94.0.s.en: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

94.0.0.en: 1- O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself.

94.0.1.en: 1- The psalmist repeats the expression “God of vengeance” twice, meaning by it the just God who repays everyone according to his works. This is evidence of his great need for God’s intervention, because he is wronged. This repetition may also be a prophecy of the coming of Christ twice: the first in His Incarnation, to take vengeance on Satan and bind him on the Cross; and the second coming, to judge the world and cast Satan and all his wicked followers into eternal torment.

94.0.2.en: 2- He calls on God to shine forth because He is the Sun of Righteousness, and he asks Him to light the world with His justice, so that the righteous may appear and be rewarded, and the wicked be punished. This shining forth is also a prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ, that He might light the world with His holiness and His redemption.

94.1.0.en: 2- Lift up thyself, thou judge of the earth: render a reward to the proud.

94.1.1.en: 1- The psalmist asks God, the only Judge of the whole earth, to lift Himself up; that is, to show His exaltation and greatness as a Judge to whom all peoples are subject. Then all the proud will fear, and God will repay them for their pride, and all the righteous who are wronged will be reassured that God the Judge will intervene and vindicate them against the proud wicked who trouble them.

94.1.2.en: 2- The lifting up of God the Judge is a prophecy of the Cross, for when Christ was lifted up on the Cross He repaid the proud, that is, the demons, and bound them by His death.

94.2.0.en: 3- LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked triumph?

94.2.1.en: Those who are wronged feel the length of the time of their oppression, and they reproach God for His long-suffering toward the sinners who gloat over them when they see the wronged in distress. The wronged forget that God is also long-suffering toward them, and they rejoice in this. So this verse is an expression of the great and urgent need of the wronged for God’s help. And God, of course, will lift the affliction from them; and if He delays for His wisdom, He comforts them and gives them peace.

94.3.0.en: 4- They utter and speak hard things: and all the workers of iniquity boast themselves.

94.3.1.en: “They utter”: they speak much; what is meant here is that they speak much evil talk.

94.3.2.en: 1- The wicked speak evil words without manners, that is, with insolence, against the righteous and against God Himself. All this is because they are proud and are not ashamed of their sins; on the contrary, they boast of them. Therefore the psalmist cries to God to stop this evil.

94.3.3.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy of what the Jews would do to Christ when they accused Him with false accusations and reviled Him with pride, and He endured all this for our sake.

94.4.0.en: 5- They break in pieces thy people, O LORD, and afflict thine heritage.

94.4.1.en: The wicked persist in their evil, so they crush the children of God, that is, the righteous, breaking them and weakening them until they lead them to despair, and the righteous are unable to resist them. Then they humble them by making them fall into lusts, and then by reproaching them for having become wicked, so that they despair. All this is directed at God personally, for Satan offends God through His children, because he says “thy people … thine heritage.” By this the psalmist stirs God to draw out His mercies, so that He may intervene and rescue His children.

94.5.0.en: 6- They slay the widow and the stranger, and murder the fatherless.

94.5.1.en: 1- The enormity of the wicked’s evils appears in their exploiting the weakness of some people, such as the widow, the stranger and the fatherless, in order to kill them; this is an excess of evil.

94.5.2.en: 2- These wicked people are the heretics, who exploit some people symbolized by the widows, since they have no support or reliance on God, so it is easy to make them fall into evil lusts. As for the stranger, he is the one who has no stability in fellowship with God, that is, his relationship with God is weak, and it is easy to kill him spiritually by drawing him away from God and making him fall into heresy. And finally the fatherless, who is a symbol of the newly converted in the faith, who can be made to doubt, so that he wavers and departs from God. This is what the scribes and Pharisees did, and Christ rebuked them for it in (Mt 23) that they might repent.

94.6.0.en: 7- Yet they say, “The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it.”

94.6.1.en: When the wicked commit the sins mentioned above and God does not punish them, they accuse Him of not seeing and not regarding, forgetting that He is long-suffering and gives them an opportunity to repent. And when they deceive themselves with this, they persist in their sins, so that in the end they deserve the divine punishment.

94.6.2.en: Do not persist in your negligence and your sins, and be careful, for God is long-suffering but just. Return to Him in repentance, for He is compassionate and will forgive you.

94.7.s.en: (2) The One who hears the complaint of the righteous

94.7.0.en: 8- Understand, ye brutish among the people: and ye fools, when will ye be wise?

94.7.1.en: The brutish and the fools are the wicked who forget the existence of God and so persist in their sins; to them are added the righteous who are weak in faith, who because of the many trials doubt their faith in God. So the psalmist stirs them to understand and believe and submit to God.

94.8.0.en: 9- He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see?

94.8.1.en: The psalmist offers simple examples that children and the simple can easily understand, to prove that God knows everything about man and observes everything that happens in the world. He says: Does the One who creates the ear and gives it the power to hear not Himself hear? And the One who creates the eye and gives it the power to see, does He not see, and see everything!

94.9.0.en: 10- He that chastiseth the heathen, shall not he correct? he that teacheth man knowledge, shall not he know?

94.9.1.en: 1- Then the psalmist offers another logical proof of God’s power and of His seeing everything. He says: if God disciplines the Gentiles who are far from faith in Him, will He not rebuke the ignorant among His people, to call them to repentance! For if He is long-suffering toward wicked men, it is so that they may repent, and, from another side, to complete His discipline of His children by means of these wicked men, so that His children may repent. From this it appears that God watches over and cares for all people, whether Jews, or Gentiles, believers or unbelievers, for all are His creation.

94.9.2.en: 2- God teaches man knowledge in the following ways:

94.9.3.en: a- He teaches His people His commandments, that they may know Him and be firm in their faith.

94.9.4.en: b- He teaches those who do not believe in Him the knowledge of Him through the conscience, which is the voice of God within them, until it leads them to faith, and they leave their sins.

94.10.0.en: 11- The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity.

94.10.1.en: God knows that most people do not believe in Him, or even that many of His children are occupied with material things instead of Him, and consequently their thoughts are tied to earthly lusts. These are vain thoughts that do not lead them to the Kingdom. Nevertheless God is long-suffering toward them that they may repent, and He may discipline them to return to Him, so that they change their thoughts, rise from material things to spiritual things, and seek God and being with Him.

94.11.0.en: 12- Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law; 13- That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity, until the pit be digged for the wicked.

94.11.1.en: On the other side, the psalm blesses the righteous man whom the Lord disciplines by allowing him trials, so that he learns the law of God, holds fast to his faith, and keeps away from evil. By this God protects him from the days of evil, that is, eternal perdition, which is the pit, or the abyss into which the wicked fall, that is, hell and the abyss. So the temporary discipline that the righteous man endures in this life keeps him from sin, binds him to God, and brings him to the Kingdom. In addition, God supports him during the afflictions of life and comforts his heart.

94.12.0.en: 14- For the LORD will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance. 15- But judgment shall return unto righteousness: and all the upright in heart shall follow it.

94.12.1.en: From the foregoing appears the justice of God, who does not leave His children in afflictions and neglect them, but supports them, comforts them, and compensates them afterward in the Kingdom. By this the perfection of justice appears after this life, when the righteous pass to the paradise of delight, and then the Kingdom of Heaven. And these are the effects of justice that the upright enjoy, that is, the joys of the Kingdom.

94.12.2.en: Do not let your heart be troubled by the afflictions that pass over you, for they are necessary to straighten your life and prepare it for the Kingdom. Trust in God’s support for you, for He protects you from Satan, gives you the victory in the end, and compensates you with what eye has not seen, that is, the glories of the Kingdom.

94.13.s.en: (3) The Comforter of the righteous and the Punisher of the wicked

94.13.0.en: 16- Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity? 17- Unless the LORD had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence.

94.13.1.en: 1- The righteous man in his distress cries out for help and rescue from the hands of the wicked who do him wrong, and he finds none, because in distress people scatter from the one in affliction. But he sees his hope in God, who does not leave him even if everyone leaves him, and sends him someone to help him, as He sent Jonathan to David to rescue him from the hands of Saul (1 Sam 19:1-7), and also sent Ebed-melech to Jeremiah to rescue him from the pit so that he would not die (Jer 38:7-13). And if God does not send a person, He gives strength to the one in trial, and inner peace, and strengthens him, as He did with Paul.

94.13.2.en: 2- God the Helper appears in the Incarnation of Christ the Redeemer, to save those who believe in Him from the hands of the evildoers and workers of iniquity, that is, the demons. And He frees His children from the land of silence, that is, the graves and death. He did not leave His children to go to eternal death, but freed them and raised them from hell to paradise.

94.14.0.en: 18- When I said, My foot slippeth; thy mercy, O LORD, held me up.

94.14.1.en: The righteous man is assured that, although he is weak as a human being and exposed to falling into sin, however great or serious, through his faith in God he trusts that God’s mercy supports him, for it calls him to repentance and then forgives him his sin. This means two things:

94.14.2.en: 1- The righteous man’s declaration, in humility, of his weakness and his need of God.

94.14.3.en: 2- His faith in God’s wide mercy, which supports him and rescues him from any sin.

94.15.0.en: 19- In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul.

94.15.1.en: The righteous man continues his speech and declares that if the cares and afflictions that come upon him increase and become very many, God does not leave him alone, but comforts his heart with sweet consolations that not only give him peace but delight him and make him enjoy fellowship with God until it makes him forget his pains. Indeed, these consolations surpass all the consolations of the earth and of men. And in proportion as the believer takes refuge in God in his distress with humble prayers and importunity, in that proportion he receives very great consolations, and in proportion to his faith he receives blessings that surpass the mind, as happened with the three youths in the furnace of fire when they saw God, and as John enjoyed the Revelation while exiled on the island of Patmos, and likewise Stephen, who saw Christ in His glory while he was being stoned.

94.16.0.en: 20- Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law? 21- They gather themselves together against the soul of the righteous, and condemn the innocent blood.

94.16.1.en: The psalmist asks a rhetorical question, saying to God: Is it reasonable that the wicked who hold power in the world would agree with You and make a covenant with You? They sit on the seat of government, authority and power, but all their deeds are corrupt and evil, and from the abundance of their corruption they make evil a statute and a law, and judge by this law against the righteous, as they did with Christ and crucified Him, and as they sentenced the Apostles to scourging and death. The answer, of course, is no: these wicked do not agree with God. In their pride they feel their authority in the world and forget God, so they walk quickly on the road to eternal perdition. Indeed, in this pride of theirs, even if they remember God they defy Him and stand as His equal and refuse to repent of their corruption and their injustice toward the righteous. By defying God they refuse God’s covenant, or submission to Him, and instead they oppose Him.

94.17.0.en: 22- But the LORD is my defence; and my God is the rock of my refuge. 23- And he shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness; yea, the LORD our God shall cut them off.

94.17.1.en: “Defence” (literally, a lofty citadel): a great, high building.

94.17.2.en: 1- The psalmist concludes his speech by saying that God is his fortress and his great refuge in which he shelters from the wicked and from all the afflictions that pass over him. He also affirms that God will punish the wicked and destroy them by casting them into eternal torment. And He brings the consequences of their evil upon their heads; that is, they are punished for every evil they have done.

94.17.3.en: 2- Christ our God, by His Incarnation and redemption, is our refuge and our strong rock, who rescues us from every evil and every affliction, lifting us above the pains, so that we feel peace and rest within the affliction, and then lifts us up to the glories of heaven.

94.17.4.en: 3- The psalm began with God as the God of vengeance in (v. 1) and ends with His destroying the wicked in (v. 23); He is a just God. And at the same time, by His justice He rewards His righteous children with sweet consolations (v. 19), and then with glories in heaven (v. 15).

94.17.5.en: Let your heart be at peace when you see injustice spreading around you, or when wrongs come upon you though you have done nothing wrong. God is just and compensates you for all your toils if you persevere with contentment, thanksgiving and steadfastness in your relationship with Him, and He supports you and then gives you joy in His fellowship forever.

94.17.6.en: Thanksgiving to God and obedience to Him: “O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation … v. 1”

94.17.8.en: 1- Its author: there are opinions on this matter

94.17.9.en: a- It has no title in the Beirut edition, that is, its author is unknown, so it is considered one of the orphan psalms.

94.17.10.en: b- St. Paul the Apostle attributes this psalm to David (Heb 4:7), and likewise in the Septuagint translation the title of this psalm says that it is David’s.

94.17.11.en: 2- When was it written? Perhaps when David moved the ark of the covenant of God from the house of Obed-edom the Gittite to Jerusalem and went before the ark with singing, dancing and sacrifices.

94.17.12.en: 3- This psalm is liturgical; it was repeated by the congregation before the Temple, especially at the dedication of the new Temple after the return from the captivity in the days of Zerubbabel and Jehozadak the high priest, and in the days of the prophets Zechariah and Haggai.

94.17.13.en: 4- This psalm is considered one of the royal psalms that speak of God the King and glorify His holy name; these psalms are (Ps 95-99), and (Ps 93) is added to them.

94.17.14.en: 5- There is a similarity between this psalm and Psalm 81 in the call to sing to the Lord, in addition to the warning against not obeying Him.

94.17.15.en: 6- This psalm was repeated when the procession moved from a holy place, such as Gihon and the Kidron Valley, which is an area east of Jerusalem, and they headed north until they entered through the gate of Jerusalem into the Temple and bowed down before it. The people would repeat the first two verses of this psalm, and the chorus, that is, the rest of the singers, would answer them with the verses (vv. 3-5); then the people would return and repeat the verse (v. 6), and the chorus would answer them with the verse (v. 7).

94.17.16.en: 7- This psalm does not occur in the prayer of the Agpeya.
